text:
Case study: Buenaventura (Buenaventura, San Juan River Delta, Colombia)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

### Case Name and Location
**El Choncho Village (New Choncho / Nuevo Choncho)**, San Juan River Delta, Pacific Coast of Colombia, Department of Chocó/Valle del Cauca, Colombia (Global South).

### Hazard(s)
The relocation was associated with coastal erosion (barrier island retreat and breaching), coastal flooding (tidal overwash and El Niño-related sea-level anomalies), coseismic land subsidence, and long-term relative sea-level rise. Regional sediment starvation due to distributary switching contributed to longer-term barrier-island instability. The proximate triggers were the breaching of the El Choncho barrier island beginning in June 1996 and the permanent inundation of its central segment by February 1998, exacerbated by coseismic subsidence associated with the November 1998 earthquake (estimated ~0.3 m subsidence at El Choncho) and El Niño 1997–1998 sea-level anomalies of 20–30 cm [Botero et al. 2013; Restrepo & López 2008].

### Type of Retreat
Community-led relocation of a small village from a rapidly eroding and flooding barrier island to a site approximately 200 meters inland on an adjacent, older, higher barrier (the Santa Barbara beaches on an ancient barrier). The relocation appears to have been initiated and implemented by the community itself, with no formal government relocation program identified in the reviewed sources. PDD (2021) classifies this as a community-initiated planned relocation case [PDD 2021].

### Scale
A small rural village. The exact number of households is listed as unknown in the PDD (2021) dataset. No specific population count is provided in the reviewed sources. Botero et al. (2013) treats it as a village-scale relocation; Martinez et al. (1995) describes the barrier island system as bearing "occasional small villages" on ocean and estuarine shores.

### Key Actors
The primary actor was the community itself. PDD (2021) identifies community actors as the initiating party. Botero et al. (2013) notes the "positive response of barrier island inhabitants to the relocation of coastal villages landward." Researchers from INGEOMINAS and EAFIT University documented the processes but did not participate in governing the relocation. No government agency, NGO, or international organization is identified in the reviewed sources as having played a governance or support role in this specific relocation.

### Timeline
- **1996 (June)**: Barrier island breached during an exceptionally high spring tide; a small channel formed and widened rapidly [Restrepo & López 2008; Botero et al. 2013].
- **December 1996–May 1997**: Channel widened to 30–50 m depth [Restrepo & López 2008].
- **December 1997**: Flooding along the central island destroyed several houses [Restrepo & López 2008].
- **February 1998**: Central part of the El Choncho island permanently inundated [Restrepo & López 2008].
- **1996–1998**: The village relocation was initiated and completed during this period [PDD 2021, Figure 7].
- **Post-1998**: New Choncho village rebuilt on the Santa Barbara beaches of the ancient barrier, approximately 200 m inland [Botero et al. 2013; PDD 2021].

### Key Outcomes
The community relocated approximately 200 meters inland to the Santa Barbara beaches on an ancient, higher barrier. Botero et al. (2013) describe this as "a positive response of barrier island inhabitants to the relocation of coastal villages landward from the actual beaches and promoting their adaptability to changes by constructing their houses entirely in wood materials." The relocation was reactive — triggered by actual island breaching — rather than proactive, and occurred with no documented government support or formal institutional planning. The hazard drivers (subsidence, sea-level rise, ENSO flooding) continue to affect the broader region. A 2022 vulnerability study of the wider Buenaventura coastal zone identifies approximately 82,008 people in areas with high to very high vulnerability to coastal erosion [Fuentes et al. 2022]; this is a regional contextual figure, not specific to El Choncho.

---

### Narrative Summary

El Choncho is a small fishing and subsistence farming community that historically occupied a low-lying barrier island on the San Juan River Delta along Colombia's Pacific coast. This coast sits on the Nazca–South American plate subduction zone, is tectonically active, mesotidal, exposed to moderate-to-high swell wave energy, and highly sensitive to El Niño-related sea-level anomalies [Botero et al. 2013; Restrepo & López 2008; Martinez et al. 1995]. The El Choncho barrier island had been experiencing chronic erosion for decades due to sand starvation — as distributary switching elsewhere in the delta reduced longshore sediment supply — with the island narrowing at approximately 1 m/year by natural progressive erosion and accelerating to an average of 11 m/year during 1993–1997 following a 1991 regional earthquake that increased flooding frequency at the site from approximately twice per year to 16 times per year [Botero et al. 2013; Restrepo & López 2008]. In June 1996, during an exceptionally high spring tide, the island was breached by a small channel that rapidly widened into a major tidal inlet. By February 1998, the central segment of the island was permanently inundated — this process was accelerated by coseismic subsidence from the November 1998 earthquake (estimated ~0.3 m at El Choncho) and by El Niño 1997–1998 sea-level anomalies of 20–30 cm above normal [Botero et al. 2013; Restrepo & López 2008].

Facing the destruction of their homes, agricultural land, and coastal plantations, the community of El Choncho decided to relocate inland — moving approximately 200 meters to the Santa Barbara beaches on an ancient, higher barrier island. The new village was rebuilt in wood construction. PDD (2021) classifies this as a community-initiated, single-origin to single-destination planned relocation, completed between 1996 and 1998. Botero et al. (2013) present it as a positive adaptive response of barrier island inhabitants to the relocation landward and to constructing houses entirely in wood.

Despite its apparent success as a community-led adaptation, the case highlights a broader pattern of institutional absence on Colombia's Pacific coast. No formal government relocation program, compensation scheme, or legal framework is identified in the reviewed sources as having facilitated the move. Botero et al. (2013) describe a fragmented institutional environment in which Colombia's main coastal authority (DIMAR) lacked explicit mandates for coastal erosion, sea-level rise, or climate change, and the Integrated Coastal Management Policy was "currently much less applied than expected." The National Programme for Coastal Erosion (INVEMAR, 2009–2019) was established years after this case and was still in early stages of implementation by 2013. Botero et al. also note that stable long-term coastal erosion monitoring did not exist in Colombia at the time. The El Choncho relocation, while locally adaptive, remains an informal, undocumented community response rather than a government-supported managed retreat program.

---

text:
Case study: Buenaventura (Buenaventura, San Juan River Delta, Colombia)
Section: CODING QUESTIONS

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer: Reactive.**

The relocation was triggered by an actual, unfolding hazard event. Restrepo & López (2008) document that: a new inlet formed in June 1996 during an exceptionally high spring tide; by December 1997, flooding along the central part of El Choncho destroyed several houses; and by February 1998, the central part of the island was permanently inundated. PDD (2021) codes the case as initiated in 1996 — after displacement had begun. The community relocated during and after the escalating destruction of their island, not in anticipation of future risk.

The underlying physical drivers (progressive erosion, subsidence following the 1991 regional earthquake, ENSO sea-level anomalies) were observable over years prior to the final breaching event, but no evidence of proactive planning, preparatory risk assessment, or pre-retreat program is found in any of the reviewed sources.

**Reactive** is the appropriate code. The evidence is consistent across all sources.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Date:** Relocation initiated approximately 1996; completed approximately 1998 [PDD 2021, Figure 7].

**Number of households:** Unknown. In the PDD (2021) dataset, the El Choncho household count is listed as unknown [PDD 2021, Figure 6]. No specific count is provided in any other reviewed source.

**Number of population affected:** Unknown. Botero et al. (2013) refer to a village-scale settlement; Martinez et al. (1995) describe the barrier islands as bearing "occasional small villages" on ocean and estuarine shores. No population count is provided in the reviewed sources. PDD (2021) notes the community included a mixed "Indians" and "Blacks" population but provides no population figure.

**Total funding:** No funding source is documented in the reviewed sources. The literature does not specify whether the move was self-financed, informally supported, or otherwise funded. PDD (2021) characterizes El Choncho as a case where community actors both initiated and planned the relocation "with only very minimal support from other actors" [PDD 2021, p. 38], but this is not a documentation of self-funding; it reflects the absence of documented external support.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer: Multiple Hazards.**

The reviewed sources document a compound and cascading hazard environment associated with this relocation:

1. **Coastal erosion** (chronic, progressive): ~11 m/year average during 1993–1997, destroying citrus and coconut plantations and houses built more than 0.5 m above highest spring tides [Restrepo & López 2008].
2. **Coastal flooding/overwash**: Frequency rose from approximately twice per year (pre-1991) to approximately 16 times per year (post-1991 earthquake) [Botero et al. 2013; Restrepo & López 2008].
3. **Coseismic land subsidence**: The November 1998 earthquake caused estimated subsidence of ~0.3 m at the central part of El Choncho barrier island [Botero et al. 2013]. The 1991 earthquake (M7.0, epicentre 40 km north of the San Juan delta) is documented as a regional hazard that increased flooding frequency across the San Juan delta area generally [Restrepo & López 2008]; it is treated here as regional background rather than an El Choncho-specific trigger.
4. **El Niño sea-level anomalies**: Positive mean sea-level anomalies of 20–30 cm along the Pacific coast of Colombia caused by El Niño 1997–1998 triggered extensive overwash and the definitive segmentation of El Choncho by widening the pre-existing channel [Botero et al. 2013; Restrepo & López 2008].
5. **Long-term relative sea-level rise**: Estimated at 2.6 mm/yr at Buenaventura [Restrepo & López 2008].
6. **Sediment starvation**: Progressive loss of sand supply due to formation of extensive sandy intertidal deltas along updrift areas, reducing longshore transport to the distal parts of the island [Botero et al. 2013].

PDD (2021) explicitly codes El Choncho as involving "coastal floods and coastal erosion, accelerated in the context of an earthquake, land subsidence and sea level rise" [PDD 2021, p. 33].

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer: Natural Hazard.**

All hazards driving the relocation are natural in origin: tectonic subsidence, seismic activity, ENSO-driven sea-level anomalies, coastal wave action, sediment transport dynamics, and long-term sea-level rise. Botero et al. (2013) explicitly state that "erosion processes on the Pacific coast are essentially due to natural phenomena, i.e. tsunami and El Niño events." No technological or anthropogenic hazard is identified as a direct driver of El Choncho's relocation in any reviewed source.

Note: Sea-level rise can be partly attributed to anthropogenic climate change, but the proximate drivers at El Choncho (seismic subsidence, tectonic setting, ENSO sea-level anomalies) are primarily natural geophysical/oceanographic processes. Climate change is not identified as the primary driver in these sources.

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process? (Select all applicable)

**Answer: Coastal Flooding/Erosion; Land Subsidence; Earthquake (as indirect/contextual driver through subsidence).**

- **Coastal Flooding/Erosion** ✓ — Primary hazard. Barrier island breaching, tidal overwash, and coastal erosion at ~11 m/year are the direct proximate causes of the relocation [Restrepo & López 2008; Botero et al. 2013].
- **Land Subsidence** ✓ — Coseismic subsidence (~0.3 m estimated at El Choncho from the November 1998 earthquake) directly exacerbated flooding frequency and erosion rates [Botero et al. 2013].
- **Earthquake** — Contextually relevant as the mechanism causing coseismic subsidence. The 1991 M7.0 earthquake contributed to regional increased flooding frequency in the San Juan delta area; the 1998 earthquake produced the estimated 0.3 m subsidence at El Choncho specifically [Botero et al. 2013; Restrepo & López 2008]. Coded as indirect/contextual.
- **Tsunami** — Contextually relevant for the broader Pacific coast (1979 Tumaco tsunami destroyed nearby San Juan de la Costa), but not a direct trigger for the 1996–1998 El Choncho relocation [Botero et al. 2013; Martinez et al. 1995].

PDD (2021) codes this case as involving coastal floods, coastal erosion, earthquake, land subsidence, and sea-level rise.

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes), (A few streets), (Neighbourhood), (Entire community), (Sub-watershed), (Watershed region)

**Answer: Entire Community.**

The relocation involved the entire village of El Choncho, which relocated as a collective unit from the eroding barrier island to the inland Santa Barbara ancient barrier. Botero et al. (2013) refer to "the New Choncho village, relocated inland." PDD (2021) codes this as a single-origin to single-destination case — consistent with a whole-community relocation. No evidence of partial or individual-only retreats is found in the reviewed sources.

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals), (Groups/Neighbourhoods), (Communities), (Critical infrastructure), (Hazard protection structures), (Industrial assets)

**Answer: Communities.**

The entire village community relocated together to the new site. PDD (2021) codes the relocating population as a community, noting that it included a mixed "Indians" and "Blacks" population. No infrastructure relocation is described in the reviewed sources.

---

### Other notes

The case is located on the San Juan River Delta barrier island system (El Choncho barrier island, also referred to as part of the San Juan barrier island group), on Colombia's Pacific coast. The new village site is on the Santa Barbara beaches on an ancient, higher barrier. The distance of relocation is approximately 200 meters [PDD 2021, Figure 5; Botero et al. 2013]. The case is situated in an area of high geodynamic hazard on the Nazca–South American plate subduction zone [Botero et al. 2013; Restrepo & López 2008]. The El Choncho barrier island formation began approximately 500 years BP according to radiocarbon dates [Botero et al. 2013].

---

text:
Case study: Buenaventura (Buenaventura, San Juan River Delta, Colombia)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat), (Community buyout/retreat), (Leasebacks, easements and buffers), (Other acquisition tools), (Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer: Community buyout/retreat** — with the important clarification that this was an informal, self-organized community relocation, not a government-administered buyout program.

The relocation was a collective community move. No formal property purchase, acquisition mechanism, compensation process, or title transfer is described in the reviewed sources. The codebook category "community buyout/retreat" is the nearest applicable code, but the notes should clarify: this was a **community-led relocation** with no documented buyout or formal acquisition instrument.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process? Are there any legal frameworks or regulations that guide the MR decision process?

**Answer: No formal legal framework, regulation, or acquisition instrument is identified in the reviewed sources for this relocation.**

None of the reviewed sources describe any legal framework, regulation, title transfer mechanism, rezoning process, or compliance requirement relevant to the El Choncho relocation specifically. PDD (2021) notes that for the majority of cases in its dataset, legal and policy frameworks were either absent or difficult to identify; El Choncho is characterized as having no identifiable normative framework.

**Broader Colombian institutional context:** Botero et al. (2013) describe a fragmented system in which: DIMAR (the national maritime authority) did not have explicit mandates for coastal erosion, sea-level rise, or climate change; the Colombian Oceanic Commission's decisions "constitute only guidelines that can be easily disregarded"; and the Integrated Coastal Management Policy was "currently much less applied than expected." Botero et al. also note that stable long-term coastal erosion monitoring did not exist in Colombia, and that the National Programme for Research, Prevention, Mitigation and Control of Coastal Erosion (INVEMAR, 2009–2019) was "hardly in its first stages of implementation" as of 2013 — well after the El Choncho relocation occurred.

No formal managed retreat policy is identified in the reviewed sources as applying to El Choncho.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer: Individual** (if one code must be selected, as relocatees appear to have been the only actors involved). However, no funding source is formally documented in the reviewed sources.

The reviewed sources do not document any funding — no government financial support, NGO contributions, international aid, or insurance mechanisms. PDD (2021) characterizes El Choncho as a case where community actors "both initiated and planned the relocation process, with only very minimal support from other actors" [PDD 2021, p. 38]. This implies the absence of documented external financial support, but does not confirm that the community self-funded the move in any specific documented manner.

**Code: Individual** — with the note that this is coded by default due to absence of evidence of any other funder, not because self-funding has been positively documented.

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer: No evidence found in reviewed sources.**

No discussion of tax base maintenance, economic development strategies, or fiscal considerations for the receiving area is found in any reviewed source. The community is a small, subsistence-oriented fishing and farming village in a remote, rural area.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer: No evidence found in reviewed sources.**

No compensation mechanism of any kind (market value, tax value, post-disaster value, additional incentives, free services, or other) is described in the reviewed sources. This was an uncompensated community relocation with no government financial support or property compensation documented.

---

text:
Case study: Buenaventura (Buenaventura, San Juan River Delta, Colombia)
Section: PLANNING PROCESSES

### What is the time horizon considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer: Immediate risks (1–5 years). No evidence of pre-retreat planning, emerging or anticipated future risk planning, or post-retreat follow-up programs.**

The relocation was reactive to immediate, unfolding hazards. The island was actively breaching and inundating between 1996 and 1998, requiring urgent relocation. There is no evidence of long-term planning horizons, climate change projections, or post-retreat follow-up programs. The time horizon was dictated by immediate physical necessity. PDD (2021) codes the case as initiated in 1996 and completed in 1998 — a roughly 2-year process — consistent with an immediate-risk reactive response.

---

### What planning elements were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer: Bottom-up (community-led); Single-stage retreat.**

The relocation was initiated and implemented by the community itself with no documented external support. Botero et al. (2013) note the "positive response of barrier island inhabitants to the relocation of coastal villages landward." PDD (2021) codes community actors as the initiating party.

**Single-stage retreat** appears to apply based on the evidence: the community moved in one general relocation phase, initiated in 1996 and completed in 1998 [PDD 2021], though direct evidence on whether movement occurred as a single event or piecemeal is limited.

No evidence found for: multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), adaptive management, top-down planning, multi-sectoral coordination, multi-stage retreat, formal transparency mechanisms, public-private partnerships, cost-benefit analysis, or formal participatory processes in any institutional sense.

---

### What decision support tools were used in the MR decision process?

**Answer: Hazard maps and models (post-hoc academic analysis only); no formal decision support tools were used in the community's own retreat decision.**

Academic researchers from INGEOMINAS and EAFIT University documented coastal changes using aerial photographs, radar imagery, field measurements, topographic profiles, and remote sensing/GIS tools [Botero et al. 2013; Restrepo & López 2008; Martinez et al. 1995]. These were scientific research and documentation tools, not tools used by the community or government to plan the retreat. The community's decision-making process is not described in the reviewed sources in terms of any formal tools. No evidence that hazard maps, CBA, demographic projections, social vulnerability assessments, site evaluation processes, or process guidance were used in the relocation decision.

Note: The community did not use these tools; the tools documented the event retrospectively.

---

### What planning measures were taken for receiving areas in the MR decision process?

**Answer: No formal planning for receiving areas documented. The community self-selected the destination site based on local knowledge.**

The community chose to relocate approximately 200 meters inland to the Santa Barbara beaches on an older, more stable ancient barrier. This choice appears to have been made based on local knowledge of the landscape. No formal site assessment, availability evaluation, housing construction by external actors, or social carrying capacity analysis is documented in the reviewed sources. Botero et al. (2013) note that houses were constructed entirely in wood at the destination site.

---

### What uses were planned for retreat lands?

**Answer: Natural use (de facto — island abandoned to natural coastal processes). No formal planning documented.**

The breached and inundated El Choncho barrier island was effectively abandoned to natural coastal processes following the relocation. No formal rezoning, demolition, conservation designation, or retreat land use planning is documented in the reviewed sources. The island continued to erode and segment naturally [Restrepo & López 2008; Botero et al. 2013]. This is not a planned outcome; it is the result of the island becoming physically uninhabitable.

**Code: Natural use** — by default, not as a deliberate planned outcome. No formal use plan is documented.

---

text:
Case study: Buenaventura (Buenaventura, San Juan River Delta, Colombia)
Section: COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT

### What degree of choice was provided to affected people in the MR decision process?

**Answer: The closest available code is Voluntary w/ strong persuasion, but this requires significant qualification.**

The community collectively decided to move and chose the destination site; no government mandate, forced eviction, or legal requirement is documented. In that formal sense, participation appears to have been voluntary. However, by February 1998, the central part of the island was permanently inundated [Restrepo & López 2008], making remaining on-site physically untenable. The "choice" was therefore severely constrained by the physical impossibility of remaining. PDD (2021) acknowledges the complexity: "overlapping sudden and slow-onset hazards constrain choices," noting that "available choices are affected by the overlap or sequential occurrence of both sudden and slow-onset hazards" [PDD 2021, pp. 9–10].

The move was community-led, but occurred under severe physical constraint as inundation made remaining on-site untenable. The codebook category "Voluntary w/ strong persuasion" is the nearest fit, but should be understood as reflecting physical necessity rather than regulatory or financial persuasion. The evidence does not support completely involuntary/mandatory, nor does it support fully free voluntary choice.

---

### What land user groups were involved or considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer: Communities (mixed indigenous and Afro-descendant); Homeowners (informal).**

PDD (2021) describes the El Choncho community as a mixed population of "Indians" and "Blacks" [PDD 2021, p. 36, footnote 89]. Fuentes et al. (2022) describes the broader Buenaventura coastal population as "demographically composed of African descendants and mixed-ancestry and indigenous communities." These are the primary land users.

Note: The sources use the terms "Indians" and "Blacks" in a historical/analytical context. PDD (2021) uses this phrasing in footnote 89, describing El Choncho. These should not be taken as formal legal designations of indigenous status. Land tenure on Colombia's Pacific coast is complex; much land may be communally held under collective territorial rights (Law 70 of 1993 for Afro-Colombian communities), but this legal dimension is not discussed in the reviewed sources in relation to this specific case.

No evidence of leased land owners, commercial operators, or government as a land user in this case.

---

### What actors participated in the governance structure of the MR decision process? Is there evidence that they shaped the MR outcomes?

**Answer: Affected community (primary decision-makers); Academics/researchers (documentation only, not governance).**

- **Affected community**: The community initiated and implemented the relocation. PDD (2021) explicitly identifies community actors as the initiating force and describes this as a case where "community members both initiated and planned the relocation process, with only very minimal support from other actors" [PDD 2021, p. 38]. Botero et al. (2013) note the community's positive adaptive response.
- **Academics/researchers**: INGEOMINAS, EAFIT University, and associated researchers documented the process retrospectively and contributed to scientific understanding, but did not participate in governance of the relocation itself.

No evidence of: funders, receiving community governance, political champions, government agencies in a governance role, private sector involvement, NGOs/CBOs, or international organizations in the relocation governance.

---

### Who ultimately made decisions in the MR decision process?

**Answer: Community.**

The community itself made the decision to relocate and chose the destination site. No government authority, property owner (in a formal Western legal sense), hazard expert, or financial institution is documented as having made decisions in this case. PDD (2021) confirms community actors as the initiating party [PDD 2021, Figure 8].

---

### Was this engagement approach explicitly incorporated into the MR decision process?

**Answer: Community engagement (informal, internal); no formal engagement mechanisms documented.**

The engagement was organic and community-internal — the village collectively decided to move and rebuilt together. No formal visualization tools, transparency mechanisms, ongoing updates, mapping processes, or structured participatory mechanisms are documented. The approach was not "explicitly incorporated" in any formal institutional sense; it was the community's own internal decision-making process.

---

### What community resources supported the transition during the MR process?

**Answer: No formal supports documented. Community relied on internal resources.**

No homeowner caseworkers, temporary housing advisors, relocation assistance payments, real estate hazard advisors, livelihood restoration programs, or community capacity-building programs are documented. Botero et al. (2013) indicate that the community constructed new houses entirely in wood at the destination site, suggesting reliance on internal labor, knowledge, and materials.

---

### What supports were provided to facilitate engagement during the MR decision process?

**Answer: No evidence found in reviewed sources.**

No psychosocial supports, caseworkers, community engagement support programs, childcare, transportation assistance, community liaisons, or technical support are documented in the reviewed sources.

---

### What language or framing was used to engage the community in the MR decision process?

**Answer: No evidence found in reviewed sources regarding the community's own framing or terminology.**

The reviewed sources do not document how the community framed or discussed the relocation process internally. Botero et al. (2013) use "relocation of coastal villages landward" in the academic description. PDD (2021) uses "planned relocation" as the analytical framework. No community-chosen terminology is documented.

**Applicable code from a research/analytical perspective: Relocation** (academic framing). No evidence of community framing as opportunity, resilience-building, or any other deliberate communication strategy.

---

text:
Case study: Buenaventura (Buenaventura, San Juan River Delta, Colombia)
Section: SOCIO-CULTURAL CONSIDERATIONS

### What special considerations for First Nations communities were included in the MR decision process?

**Answer: No formal considerations documented in the reviewed sources.**

PDD (2021) describes the El Choncho community as mixed "Indians" and "Blacks" [PDD 2021, p. 36, footnote 89]. These groups hold significant cultural and, in Colombia's legal framework, collective territorial rights. However, none of the reviewed sources describe any formal consideration of:
- Indigenous governance systems or decision-making protocols
- Non-market values of land
- Place attachment (though the community's choice to relocate only 200 m inland may reflect it)
- Ancestral lands protections
- Cultural or sacred site considerations
- Historical forced relocation context
- Collective territorial rights

The absence of government involvement means these considerations were neither formally addressed nor formally violated in the retreat process itself. This represents a significant documentation gap. The codebook note for this case should read: "No formal Indigenous governance/protocol considerations are documented in the reviewed sources."

---

### What equity considerations were addressed in the MR decision process?

**Answer: No formal equity considerations documented. Significant implicit equity concerns exist but were not addressed through any program.**

The community affected is among the most marginalized in Colombia: mixed Afro-descendant and indigenous, living in conditions of significant poverty and remoteness. Fuentes et al. (2022) document that approximately 33.3% of Buenaventura's coastal population lives below the poverty level, and that the coastal zone is characterized by "insufficient resources, multidimensional poverty, and remoteness." The retreat was uncompensated and unsupported by any government program.

Equity dimensions present but unaddressed in this case:
- **Vulnerable and marginalized community members**: A highly marginalized minority group with limited resources bore the full burden of relocation.
- **No compensation**: Households lost homes and livelihood infrastructure without any financial support.
- **Homeowners vs. renters vs. communal owners**: Land tenure complexity on Colombia's Pacific coast (collective territorial rights under Law 70 of 1993) was not addressed in the reviewed sources.
- **Continued access to services in new location**: No evidence that access to services at the new location was assessed or improved.

---

### What resilience, Build Back Better (BBB), or disaster risk reduction (DRR) goals were achieved through the MR decision process?

**Answer: Reduced hazard exposure (well supported); Increased community resilience (plausible, moderately supported); Maintain/enhance social capital (inferred from collective relocation, not directly documented); Maintain/enhance healthy ecosystems (incidental, not planned).**

- **Reduced hazard exposure** ✓ — The community moved from an actively breaching, permanently inundating barrier island to more stable higher ground approximately 200 meters inland. This directly reduced exposure to coastal flooding, wave erosion, and island breaching.
- **Increased community resilience** ✓ — The community demonstrated adaptive capacity by relocating collectively and reconstructing using locally appropriate wood construction techniques suited to the coastal environment. Botero et al. (2013) present this as a positive adaptive response, highlighting the construction of houses entirely in wood.
- **Maintain/enhance social capital** — Inferred from collective relocation (the community moved together, preserving social networks), but not directly documented as an outcome in the reviewed sources. Should be treated as plausible but not confirmed.
- **Maintain/enhance healthy ecosystems** — The vacated barrier island returned to natural processes, though this was not a planned ecosystem restoration outcome. Not attributable as a planned DRR goal.
- **Maintain/enhance housing quality/stock** — Housing was rebuilt in wood. Whether this constitutes an improvement over previous conditions is not directly assessed in the reviewed sources.

NOT achieved or not documented: resilient infrastructure, tax base maintenance or enhancement, formal DRR planning integration.

---
